metaTitle: Best 8 Gallon RV Water Heaters in 2026
metaDescription: Six 8 gallon 120V electric tank water heaters used in RVs, campers and food trucks, compared on tank material, wattage, mounting and safety valves.
expertTake: The VEVOR is the pick for a camper or food trailer on shore power because it carries a temperature and pressure safety valve and a stainless tank at the lowest price tier here. The Ariston is the choice if you want an established brand name. Anyone who boondocks on propane should skip all of these, since they need 120V and burn no gas.
introParagraphs: Eight gallons is a size that rarely appears on traditional propane RV heaters, which come in six, ten and twelve. The eight gallon machines sold for campers are small electric tanks borrowed from the residential under-sink world, and they behave quite differently.

That difference decides everything: they need a household-voltage supply, they have no burner or vent, and they are sized for a sink or a short shower rather than a family. Matching one to a trailer means checking power, plumbing and safety hardware before looking at brand.

products.name: VEVOR 8 Gallon Electric Mini-Tank Water Heater, 1440W, TP Valve
products.description:
VEVOR combines a stainless steel tank, a 1440W element and a temperature and pressure safety valve in a package at the lowest price tier of the group. The safety valve is the detail that matters most: a sealed tank that heats water must have a relief path, and a valve that is included means you are less likely to improvise one.

Stainless steel avoids the rust-through risk of a thin steel tank, and a 1440W element draws about 12 amps at 120V, which fits a 15 amp circuit with little to spare. In a trailer on a 30 amp service you can run it with a modest load, but a microwave and air conditioner at the same time will trip the breaker.

The tradeoff is documentation: VEVOR does not state a recovery time or an insulation rating, so assume roughly an hour to heat a full tank from cold at 1440W. It is wall or floor mounted, so measure the cabinet before you buy. Never plug the relief valve outlet, and run the discharge to a safe drain.
products.bestFor: Camper and trailer owners on shore power who want a safety valve included.

products.name: Ariston Andris 8 Gallon Mini Tank Electric Water Heater, 120V

specList.label: Install modes
specList.value: Stand-alone or booster to an existing heater

specList.label: Intended use
specList.value: Under sink, RV and similar spaces

products.description:
Ariston is an established name in small electric water heaters, and the Andris is a familiar choice for tiny spaces. Its tank has a titanium glass lining, which protects the steel shell from the water, and the listing explicitly offers installation as a stand-alone unit or as a booster ahead of an existing heater.

The booster role is the underrated feature for an RV. If your main heater is slow to recover or far from a bathroom, a small electric tank near the sink can raise water temperature close to the tap, so you get hot water without waiting for the long pipe run to clear. That use also keeps the 120V draw intermittent.

It sits in the upper-middle price tier, above the VEVOR and BISELONG, because you are paying for the maker's reputation and parts support. The listing does not state a wattage in the details we have, so confirm it against the sticker before you plan the circuit. Plumb it with flexible lines so a rough road does not stress the fittings.
products.bestFor: Owners who want an established maker and may use it as a booster.
pros: Can be a stand-alone unit or a booster
cons: Wattage not stated in the listing details
No temperature and pressure valve mentioned

products.name: Feelrogast 8 Gallon Under-Sink Electric Tank Heater for RVs

specList.label: Safety
specList.value: Leakage protection plug and high-temperature limiter

products.description:
Feelrogast aims this model straight at RV, camper and food-truck buyers, and the safety list is thorough: a leakage protection plug, electrical insulation on the inlet and outlet and a high-temperature limiting device. A plug that trips on a ground fault is a sensible addition in a vehicle where wet floors and metal frames share space.

The tank wall is 1.88 mm stainless steel, thinner than the 2.0 mm on the BISELONG, though both are in the same class. The listing cites CE, RoHS and FCC marks, which are electromagnetic and materials standards, not a US plumbing or electrical safety listing, so read them as limited assurance.

It sits at a low price tier, between the VEVOR and the BISELONG. A sister listing from the same maker has a 4 and 8 gallon pair of sizes, so confirm you are buying the 8 gallon version. Keep the leakage plug accessible so you can test it, and mount the unit where road vibration will not strain the supply lines.
products.bestFor: Camper and food-trailer owners who want built-in leakage protection.
pros: Marketed and sized for RV use
cons: Thinner tank wall than the BISELONG
CE, RoHS and FCC are not US safety listings
Similar listings in other sizes can confuse buyers

products.name: BISELONG 8 Gallon 1500W Electric Tank Heater for RV and Trailers

specList.label: Mounting
specList.value: Wall, rack or floor, with 1/2 inch NPT to 3/8 inch fittings

products.description:
BISELONG has the thickest listed tank wall of the stainless units, 2.0 mm, and a 316 stainless steel heating element, a grade chosen for corrosion resistance. The listing claims 99 percent thermal efficiency, which should be read as the element converting nearly all of its electricity to heat, a property of any resistance heater, not as a claim about standby losses.

Mounting is the real selling point. It can go on a wall, on a rack or on the floor, and it ships with adapters from a 1/2 inch NPT thread to 3/8 inch fittings, which is useful because many RV plumbing runs use small-diameter lines. The 1500W element draws 12.5 amps, a little more than the VEVOR, so budget your circuit accordingly.

It lands near the bottom of the price tiers, just above the VEVOR. Compared with the Feelrogast, it lacks the leakage-protection plug on the listing but offers more mounting options. As with every unit here, install a pressure relief valve if one is not supplied and never plug it.
products.bestFor: Awkward cabinets where wall, rack or floor mounting matters.
cons: 1500W draw is the highest of the six
Relief valve not highlighted on the listing

products.name: thermomate 8 Gallon Electric Tank Heater, 1440W, Porcelain Lined
products.description:
thermomate takes a different route from the stainless units: a three-layer tank lined with fused porcelain enamel glass. This is the same lining approach used in conventional home water heaters, which protects the steel shell from water, and the listing cites a 10,000 impulse test to show the tank can handle pressure cycling.

A 1440W plug-in design is easy to live with, and the unit can mount on a wall or sit on the floor. A glass-lined steel tank is typically paired with a sacrificial anode rod in conventional heaters, but the listing does not mention one, so ask the seller before you assume you need to service it.

Price-wise, it lands in the upper-middle price tier, a bit above the Ariston, so you pay for the lining story rather than for features. If you tow on rough roads, a stainless tank tolerates flexing better than a glass lining, so consider where the trailer spends its time. For a stationary camper on a lot, this is a reasonable pick.
products.bestFor: Stationary campers and cabins where a glass-lined tank is acceptable.
cons: Anode rod status is not stated
Glass lining is less forgiving of road flex than stainless

products.name: Electrolux 8 Gallon Plug-In Under-Sink Electric Water Heater
products.description:
Electrolux sells this as a compact point-of-use heater, with an enamel-coated inner tank and a plug that goes into a standard outlet. The listing stresses easy do-it-yourself installation with no gas line and no heavy electrical work, which is true for any plug-in unit and appealing in a small camper.

It is not an RV-specific product, so treat the RV question as your own. A household appliance in a moving vehicle sees vibration and a tilting floor that a stationary home never does, so secure it firmly with straps or brackets, and use flexible hoses at both connections.

It carries the highest price tier among the six, and the premium is for the brand name rather than RV features. The Feelrogast and BISELONG cost less and list more RV-oriented hardware. Buy the Electrolux when the unit will live in a stationary cabin, a tiny house or a garage workshop instead of a moving trailer.
products.bestFor: Stationary cabins and tiny houses that want a brand-name plug-in unit.
pros: Plug-in design with no gas line
cons: Highest price tier in the group
Needs secure mounting in a moving vehicle

buyingCriteria.explanation: Every unit here is a 120V resistance heater with no burner, vent or 12V ignition. A gas-electric RV heater runs on propane as well and does not need shore power. If you camp off the grid, the eight gallon electrics will only work when you run a generator or plug in. Check your supply before you buy.

The VEVOR and thermomate draw 1440W, about 12 amps, and the BISELONG and Feelrogast 1500W, about 12.5 amps. On a 15 amp circuit that leaves almost nothing for other loads, and even a 30 amp RV service can be strained when an air conditioner starts. Plan to run the heater on its own circuit or at off-peak times.

Stainless steel tanks, like the VEVOR's 310S and the BISELONG's 2.0 mm wall, resist corrosion and do not need an anode rod. Glass-lined steel, as on the thermomate and Ariston, relies on the lining staying intact. Road vibration can stress a lining, so stainless suits a vehicle that moves.

A sealed tank must have a temperature and pressure relief path, and the VEVOR includes one on its listing. The Feelrogast adds a leakage protection plug and a high-temperature limiter. Never plug or cap a relief valve, and run its discharge to a drain you can see.

Eight gallons gives about two short showers or several sink-loads when mixed with cold water. Recovery from cold at roughly 1500W takes about an hour. A one-person weekend fits easily, but a family of four will run out, so check the size against your habits.

RV plumbing usually uses small PEX or flexible lines. The BISELONG ships with adapters from 1/2 inch NPT to 3/8 inch, and the Ariston and thermomate use standard fittings. Strap the tank down and use flexible hoses, since a rigid connection can crack on a rough road.

specDecoder.meaning: Amps equal watts divided by volts, so 1500W at 120V is 12.5 amps. A 15 amp breaker trips above 15 amps, and a continuous load should stay under about 80 percent of the breaker rating.
specDecoder.watchFor: BISELONG at 1500W and VEVOR at 1440W both fit, but leave little room.

specDecoder.meaning: Thicker stainless resists denting and pressure cycling better. It also adds weight, which matters for a trailer's tongue and axle balance.
A relief device that opens if the tank gets too hot or too pressurized, preventing a rupture. Water also expands as it heats, so the valve or an expansion tank is required.
specDecoder.watchFor: Only the VEVOR names a valve on its listing.

specDecoder.meaning: A coating of glass fused to the steel to keep water from touching the metal. If it chips, the steel can rust, and conventional tanks use an anode rod for backup.
specDecoder.watchFor: thermomate and Ariston use glass-type linings.

specDecoder.meaning: A 99 percent figure usually describes the element turning power into heat, which is true of any resistance heater. It says nothing about how well the tank holds that heat.
specDecoder.watchFor: BISELONG and Feelrogast both cite 99 percent.

howWeEvaluated.title: Honest category
howWeEvaluated.description: We kept only 8 gallon tank heaters and dropped the Suburban 10 gallon propane unit and the tankless models, since the keyword names the size. We also noted that all six are 120V electrics, not gas RV heaters.

howWeEvaluated.title: Safety hardware
howWeEvaluated.description: Using the stated specs, we ranked relief valves, leakage protection plugs and temperature limiters. The VEVOR's valve and the Feelrogast's plug and limiter scored well, while listings that mention neither lost points.

howWeEvaluated.title: Tank construction
howWeEvaluated.description: Stainless steel units were weighed for corrosion resistance and wall thickness, with the BISELONG's 2.0 mm wall ranking above the Feelrogast's 1.88 mm. Glass-lined tanks were judged on how they handle vibration.

howWeEvaluated.title: Electrical load
howWeEvaluated.description: Wattage was converted to amps and compared with a 15 amp circuit. The 1440W units draw about 12 amps and the 1500W units about 12.5, and none leave much margin.

howWeEvaluated.title: Owner feedback patterns
howWeEvaluated.description: Owner remarks that keep recurring were weighed: fittings that leak after a bumpy trip, tanks that arrive without a relief valve, and the shock of how little hot water eight gallons gives. Setup mistakes are more common than outright failures.

cards.label: Stainless
cards.text: The VEVOR, Feelrogast and BISELONG use stainless tanks, which resist corrosion and tolerate vibration. They are the sensible choice for a trailer that moves, and they do not rely on a sacrificial anode rod.

cards.label: Glass-lined
cards.text: The thermomate, Ariston and Electrolux use glass or enamel linings, a proven method for home heaters. A chip in the lining can lead to rust, so these suit stationary installations better than a trailer on rough roads.

howToChoose.note: Pick stainless for a moving rig and glass-lined for a cabin or tiny house.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A propane or gas-electric heater of six to ten gallons is the normal answer for full-time living. If you stay on shore power, an eight gallon electric works for one or two people, with a relief valve, strapped mounting and flexible hoses.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The VEVOR is the best match for a shore-power setup because of its included safety valve and low price tier. The Ariston is the alternative as a booster at a sink far from the main heater.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You want an established maker and local support, or the unit will be a permanent fixture. The Ariston and Electrolux justify their tiers with brand backing, not extra features.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: The rig is a weekend camper on shore power. The VEVOR, BISELONG or Feelrogast supply eight gallons at a low tier, and the savings pay for flexible hoses and a second relief valve.

maintenance.why: Vibration loosens connections and can crack rigid lines. A quick check prevents a flooded cabinet.
Sediment lowers efficiency and causes rumbling noises. Drain through the valve and rinse until the water runs clear.
A stuck valve is a safety risk. Lift the lever briefly and confirm that water flows to the drain.
Water left in the tank expands when frozen and can split the shell. Drain it fully and leave a valve open.
A hot plug or a damaged cord on a 12 amp load is a fire risk. Replace anything warm to the touch.

faq.q: Are these real RV water heaters?
faq.a: They are electric point-of-use tank heaters that people install in RVs, campers and food trucks. They are not propane units, and none lights a burner. Check that your electrical supply can carry the load.

faq.q: How much hot water does eight gallons give?
faq.a: About two short showers or several sink-loads when mixed with cold water. A weekend trip for one or two people is fine, but a family of four will run out.

faq.q: How long does it take to heat a full tank?
faq.a: From cold, roughly an hour at 1440 to 1500W, since a gallon of water needs about 0.2 kilowatt hours to rise by 70 degrees. A running tank holds heat between uses.

faq.q: Do I need a relief valve?
faq.a: Yes. A sealed tank that heats water needs a temperature and pressure relief path, and water expands as it warms. Only the VEVOR names one on its listing, so add one if yours does not include it.

faq.q: Can I run it off a generator or solar?
faq.a: A generator that can supply 1500 watts continuously can run it. A solar and battery system would need a large inverter, so most owners run these only on shore power or a generator.
Shut off the power, drain the tank fully, open a faucet and leave a drain valve open. Never leave water in the tank in freezing weather, since expanding ice can split the shell.
